extracted.intended_audience: higher-education instructors, instructional designers and researchers developing/evaluating MOOCs (particularly mathematics/foundational-skills MOOCs)
extracted.subtask_short: MOOC design and evaluation for math refresher
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating a task- and resource-based MOOC aimed at non-expert or stressed mathematics learners, including choice of pedagogy, scaffolded learning sequence, OER use, analytics and qualitative evaluation. Emphasis on foundational math skills refresher courses in university/community contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit for purpose / alignment with aims and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the design suitable and aligned with the aims of the MOOC, its learning outcomes and intended audience? 'Whether the MOOC is fit for purpose... is the design suitable and aligned with the aims of the MOOC, its learning outcomes and intended audience?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider discipline-specific issues in design; ask whether the learning objectives can be met by the intended learners and whether the MOOC can assist with issues particular to the academic discipline. Design choices (e.g. content vs collaboration focus) should be driven by intended learner expertise (novice vs advanced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of scaffolding to support low self-efficacy learners
rubrics_metrics.description: High degrees of scaffolding are suitable and helpful to deal with low self-efficacy and stress in maths learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide gradual reduction in teacher support across a learning sequence so students progress from teacher demonstration to independent practice; use scaffolding particularly when learners report anxiety or low confidence. Link to literature on self-efficacy as a key predictor of learning success (Bandura).

rubrics_metrics.name: Task-based vs content/networking balance (MOOC taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a task- and resource-based MOOC design where content, tasks and networking/social learning are not mutually exclusive but complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a taxonomy (Lane 2012) rather than a strict xMOOC/cMOOC dichotomy; select primary focus (content, tasks, or networked learning) while allowing complementary elements to be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for non-expert/stressed learners while allowing expert participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design targeted at non-expert and/or stressed maths learners with highly scaffolded and structured learning space, yet flexible enough for experts to dip into challenging material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear learning pathways and optional deeper material; allow learners to choose how much to engage depending on needs. Expect a mixed cohort and design to accommodate different motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Open Educational Resources and openness principles (four 'R's)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt OER practices following David Wiley's four 'R's model (re-use, redistribute, revise, remix) when building the MOOC and selecting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer Creative Commons licensed resources, link to openly licensed textbooks and video resources, and design materials that others can adapt and redistribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video-quiz formative feedback design (stop-points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Video quizzes that break problems into parts with 'stop points' where learners must answer before continuing, followed by immediate worked-method feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Video quizzes provide greater scaffolding and formative feedback than standard quizzes; include 3-4 stop points per video to recap technique, test understanding, and show correct methods after each attempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit learning sequence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a consistent weekly learning sequence: (1) theory refresher video; (2) worked examples with increasing difficulty; (3) video quizzes; (4) substantial practice task ('test yourself: practice questions' / assignment); (5) optional higher-level assignment (create a video lesson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence demonstrates scaffolding from teacher demonstration to student independent practice; keep navigation simple (e.g. pull-down menu) to allow selective engagement by learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-paced access and learner choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow learners to move through the program at their own pace and to choose which items to engage with depending on goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design navigation and materials so students can start with quizzes, worked examples, or theory as needed; self-pacing can be more effective than face-to-face for some learners because they can pause and reflect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional peer engagement and limited facilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide optional channels for peer interaction (Facebook group, email group) and make online coaching available, recognizing some learners need or want community encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep peer spaces optional and private if desired; expect small engaged subgroups (e.g. a few dozen followers) and occasional facilitator input that can positively impact persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation using enrolment and demographic data
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect demographic data at enrolment (age, location, native language, time since last maths study, reason for enrolment) to understand cohort composition and motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-text fields to capture motivations and anxiety information; demographic breakdowns can reveal which subgroups engage more with assignments (e.g. mature learners, 'a bit stressed' learners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation using analytics and usage data
rubrics_metrics.description: Use web analytics (Google Analytics, YouTube stats, page views) to gauge patterns of use and engagement across weeks and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare unique webpage views for theory, worked examples, video quizzes, and assignments; track drop-off across weeks and identify pages that maintain interest (e.g. assignment pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment submission and completion rate as a success metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the percentage of students who submit the practice assignment per module as an indicator of engagement and completion (e.g. observed 18.3% vs expected ~10% for MOOCs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use submission rates averaged across modules to compare to benchmark MOOC completion expectations; analyze which learner segments submit at higher rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment performance/marks distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse assignment marks (median marks, % achieving 60%/70% thresholds, distribution across modules) to assess mastery of topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report module-level statistics (median, % above thresholds, notable high-distinction rates) and compare assignment cohort performance to whole cohort to detect selection effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative feedback and open-text responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect qualitative feedback via forms at assignment submission to capture learner perceptions of usefulness, engagement, and specific resource value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use learner quotes to identify valued features (videos, breakdown of working, pacing, 'better than face-to-face') and to guide future development priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing, branding and recruitment strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ catchy course title, humorous graphics and targeted promotions (media releases, digital signage, flyers, emails to partners) to attract learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong brand aids visibility in internal and external media; leveraging partner networks and faculty referrals increases enrolment without large budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing math anxiety and face-saving learning opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Design elements that allow private practice (attempt problems in private) to reduce feelings of 'I'm dumb' and to provide a face-saving way to learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities for learners to attempt practice before seeing answers, and consider submission-before-answers mechanics to encourage earnest attempts and protect learner dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility for disciplinary customisation and future expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan to expand topics and customise content for different disciplines to contextualise why selected maths skills matter for particular professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage faculty from relevant professions to prioritise extensions; contextualised examples can increase perceived relevance and uptake in discipline-specific cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility, scalability and resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider production effort and budget (e.g. course developed over 2 months by one staff member with a small casual-budget for video quizzes) when planning a MOOC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether online format allows supporting more learners than face-to-face; small budgets can still produce effective scaffolded resources if reuse of existing OERs is leveraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment design to promote serious engagement (submission-before-answers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require submission of an indicative sample of questions before providing worked solutions to ensure learners attempt problems seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use web forms to collect sample submissions and then automatically provide links to answers; this balances learner need for feedback with encouraging genuine effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional higher-order assignment (learner-generated content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer an optional assignment asking students to create their own video lesson as an advanced/reflective task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide resources and tutorials for media production; such tasks can deepen learning but may attract few submissions and can be outside initial evaluation scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of worked examples and progressive difficulty in worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide short video lessons showing a mathematician solving problems at the whiteboard, starting with easy examples before moving to more complex ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples should be sequenced to build confidence and technique; pairing with video quizzes and practice problems reinforces mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner segmentation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare characteristics of the whole cohort to the subset who engage deeply (assignment cohort) to understand who benefits and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment by age, time since last maths study, stress level, reason for enrolment, and language to identify over- or under-represented groups among active participants.
